title: Influence of perioperative Inflammation on metabolic processes (CYP3A-activity) in patients undergoing elective surgery – a pilot study
summary:
In humans, more than half of all drugs on the market are broken down by a specific protein (cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A). These include many substances that are used for general anaesthesia or post-operative treatment (e.g. shielding in intensive care units, blood thinning, suppression of the immune system after organ transplantation). These drugs often have narrow limits within which they must be dosed, otherwise they will not work or may be harmful to the patient. Changes in the amount of drug in the body of 50 % can therefore be clinically relevant.
It is known that inflammation in the body releases messenger substances (cytokines) that inhibit CYP3A within a few days and reduce its activity by approx. 60 % of its initial activity. Such a reduction in CYP3A capacity can lead to a multiplication of the blood concentration of drugs that are broken down by CYP3A, e.g. in the context of organ function restrictions after surgery (e.g. kidney failure). Particularly in the case of drugs with narrow dosage limits, this can have harmful consequences for the patients concerned.
In surgical interventions, the associated tissue destruction leads to the release of immune-activating cell components (so-called ‘damage-associated molecular patterns’). As with an infection, these lead to an activation of the immune system. To date, it is not known whether and to what extent this perioperative, and in some cases even systemic, inflammatory reaction influences CYP3A activity in real patient groups. There is a lack of clinical studies to help identify patients at particular risk. 
In this study, the CYP3A activity of the patient (‘phenotype’) is determined during and after surgery at specific time points by oral administration of midazolam. At the same time, the ‘immune phenotype’ is determined in blood samples from the patients. CYP3A activity and immune phenotype will be correlated during the perioperative course.
Ultimately, these data should provide a building block for the personalisation and optimisation of drug therapy and drug therapy safety in the high-risk environment of anaesthesia and intensive care medicine.

interventions.name: assessment of the influence of perioperative inflammation of elective operations on CYP3A-activity (midazolam phenotyping): CYP phenotyping: 0 h , 48 h, 7 d.  characterisation of immune system: pre-OP, post-OP: 4 h, 24 h, 48 h, 7 d or prior to discharge.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
-Patients with major elective visceral surgery requiring general, neuraxial or regional anaesthesia,
-Patients with an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) classification of 1-3 at the time of the examination,
-Capable of giving written, personally signed and dated informed consent to participate in the study in accordance with the International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH) guideline E6 on Good Clinical Practice (GCP) and applicable regulations prior to any procedures associated with the study.
Exclusion criteria:
1. emergency operations,
2. planned liver resection or transplantation,
3. acute hepatitis,
4. ASA 4 and 5 at the time of the examination,
5. any autoimmune disease (including type I diabetes),
6. dialysis-dependent renal failure,
7. pregnancy or breastfeeding, or
8. respiratory insufficiency and depression; or
9. any known history of severe allergic or anaphylactic reaction to midazolam
10. regular use of known strong CYP3A inducers (e.g. rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, St John's wort),
11. regular intake of known strong CYP3A inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, clarithromycin, erythromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit juice)
12. blood haemoglobin values < 10 g/d, or
13. general refusal to participate in the study.
